newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul stocks close higher on technical rebound.
newsitem.headline: Seoul stocks close higher on technical rebound.

text.p: Seoul stocks closed Wednesday higher on a broad-based technical rebound, but brokers said investor jitters about more corporate failures still clouded the wobbly market.
Ssangyong Group strongly denied rumours of cash flow problems but the denial was not good enough to soothe nervous investors. Most Ssangyong group shares went limit down.
The composite stock index rose 4.60 points to 730.58.
"It's just a technical rebound following steep declines," said Ha Sung-won at Ssangyong Securities. "Kia and Ssangyong issues continued to cool down market sentiment."

Brokers said some large-capitalised shares were in strong demand. LG Electronics rose 800 won to 17,900 and LG Chemical went limit up to 14,100, up 1,000, with the day's largest trading volume of 1.07 million shares.

LG Metals Corp rose to its upper limit to 17,200 won after the company reported increased earnings in the first half. LG Metals said its six-month current profit rose to 28.5 billion won against a 7.0 billion loss a year earlier.
"The market needs more time to be stabilised from the initial shock by Kia and rumoured Ssangyong problems," said Park Ki-pyong at Hanyang Securities.

Financially troubled Kia Group continued its self-rescue plan, raising 350 billion won in the past three days through cash discount car sales. The ruling New Korea Party urged the government on Wednesday to take action to resolve Kia's woes.
Kia shares were mixed. Kia Motors ended unchanged at 12,100 won and Asia Motors rose 100 won to 3,510.

Brokers forecast jitters about Ssangyong would eventually ease as the group was different from Kia. They said Ssangyong looked be in good shape except for its automaking unit, while Kia had few profit-making affiliates.
But nine of the 10 listed Ssangyong shares went limit down.
Ssangyong Motors briefly hit a 1997 low of 3,990 but rebounded to close at 4,050, down 280.
Ssangyong Paper lost 1,400 won to 16,100 and Ssangyong Cement shed 750 won to 8,650.
"Investors will take a conservative attitude toward Kia until they can see a clear sign of the group's future," Ha of Ssangyong said.

After the market close, Standard & Poor's credit-rating agency said it had placed five Korean banks on Credit Watch with negative implications, reflecting deteriorating asset quality and heightening industry risks faced by Korean banks.
The credit rating company said it was concerned about the potential for spillover of defaults to other sectors of the economy and ultimately to the banking sector.
"This will affect the banking shares tomorrow. Foreign investors especially will take the news seriously," said Park of Hanyang Securities.
But some brokers said domestic investors would stick to their long-standing belief that the government would never let banks to go bankrupt.
